title: Joining and Writing Sentences
overview: Join two ideas with but, or and then. Put capitals on names, places and days. End with a full stop or a question mark. Plan, write and check a note, a list or a postcard. The quiz also checks Units 7 to 12.
learningPath: Words: listen, look and say. 23 words.
Patterns: 4 cards. Read the one done for you.
Reading: a story, a guide and a notice.
Speaking: tap the mic. Say it. Listen.
Writing: plan, write, check. Made-up is OK.
Practice: write. Check with the answers.
Quiz: 12 questions, some from Units 7 to 12.
lectureScript:
Hello! This is Unit 13.
This unit is about writing.
You join ideas. You write notes, lists and postcards.
The quiz has questions from Units 7 to 12 too.
First, joining words. You know and.
I like tea and coffee.
Now three more: but, or, then.
But: the two ideas are different.
I like tea, but I don't like coffee.
Or: you choose one.
Tea or coffee?
We can walk, or we can take the bus.
Then: this one comes after.
I did my homework. Then I went to bed.
Say a small stop before but. Write a comma there.
Now capital letters. Where do they go?
On the first word of every sentence.
On names: Nadia, Tomas.
On the names of places: Park Street, the Star Café.
On days and months: Monday, June.
On a language: English.
The word I is always a capital.
A street or a café with no name is small.
Now the end of a sentence.
A sentence that tells ends with a full stop.
The class is on Monday. Full stop.
A sentence that asks ends with a question mark.
Is the class on Monday? Question mark.
Where, when, do, did and can start questions.
In a list, put a comma between the things.
Bread, milk and eggs.
A comma after bread. Before and, no comma.
Now, three steps for a short note.
Step one: plan. Who is it for? Why do you write it?
Write your ideas as a list.
Step two: write. One idea in each sentence.
Join some ideas with and, but, or and then.
Step three: check. Read it again, line by line.
Look for one thing at a time.
First capitals. Then full stops and question marks. Then spelling.
Not sure of a word? Look in a dictionary.
A mistake is OK. Find it, then fix it.
Write by hand too.
Make your small letters all one size.
Leave a space between two words.
In Reading, Nadia leaves her notebook at a café. Does she get it back?
Now go to Words. Goodbye!

outcomes.outcome: Join two words or two ideas with and, but, or and then, and put a comma before but.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 1 practice self-checked; Practice 1 and 2; Writing 1 checklist; Quiz items 1 to 3.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can join two ideas with but, or and then.

outcomes.outcome: Say two ideas as one sentence, and tell an evening step by step with then.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 1 and 2 recordings, each against its checklist.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can say what I did, step by step, with then.

outcomes.outcome: Put capitals on names, places, days, months, languages, I and the first word, and write by hand with letters of one size and a space between words.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 2 practice; Practice 3 and 5; Writing 3 checklist; Quiz items 4 and 5.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can put capitals on names, places and days.

outcomes.outcome: End a sentence that tells with a full stop and a sentence that asks with a question mark, and use commas in a list.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 3 practice; Practice 4; Writing 4 checklist; Speaking 5 recording; Quiz items 6 and 7.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can end a sentence with a full stop or a question mark.

outcomes.outcome: Plan, write and check a short note or postcard, and check a new word in a dictionary.
outcomes.evidence: Pattern 4 practice; Writing 2 checklist; Reading 2 questions; Quiz item 8.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can plan, write and check a short note.

outcomes.outcome: Read a short story, a guide and a notice, and say the main point and the details a reader needs.
outcomes.evidence: Reading questions 1 to 10; Writing 4, where every answer comes from the notice.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can read a short story and say what it is about.

outcomes.outcome: Follow a short list of spoken steps for a writing task.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 4: the paper compared line by line with its model.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can listen to four steps and do them.

outcomes.outcome: Ask and answer short questions with or, do, did and can, using the patterns of Units 7 to 12.
outcomes.evidence: Speaking 3 and 6 recordings; Practice 6; Quiz items 9 to 12.
outcomes.cefrDescriptor: I can ask and answer at a desk: When is it? Can I borrow one?

words.meaning: A short message on paper, for a person to read.
words.example: I left a note on the fridge for Omar.
practice: Read the note on the door.
Can you write a note for Sam?
The note says: Back at six.
I found a note in my bag.
Her note has three short lines.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor who your note is for and why. Write it in three lines, then ask it to check that each line ends with a full stop.

words.meaning: A card with a photo. You send it to a friend from a place you visit.
words.example: I sent a postcard from the city.
practice: The postcard has a photo of a big park.
Did you get my postcard?
Write the address on the postcard.
I got two postcards at the post office.
My postcard is for Zoe.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor about a made-up place you visited. Say three things for a postcard from there, with a capital on each place name.

words.meaning: Words one under the other, like the things to get at the shop.
words.example: My list for the shop: bread, milk and eggs.
practice: Put rice on the list.
Is tea on your list?
I have a list of new words.
The list is on the fridge.
A list has a comma between the things.
words.tutor: Say four things for the shop. Ask the tutor to write them as one list, then check: a comma between the things, and and before the last one.

words.meaning: A paper with questions. You write your name, address and phone number on it.
words.example: Please write your name on the form.
practice: The library form asks for your address.
Did you finish the form?
Write in capital letters on this form.
I got a form at the desk.
The form has six questions.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to be the person at a desk and read four questions from a made-up form. Answer each one with made-up details.

words.meaning: Words together that tell or ask one thing. It starts with a capital letter.
words.example: I like tea. This sentence has three words.
practice: Write one sentence about your day.
Start every sentence with a capital letter.
Read the first sentence again.
My sentence ends with a full stop.
Join two sentences with but.
words.tutor: Give the tutor five words in a mixed order, milk, tea, I, and, like. Put them in order yourself, and ask it if your sentence is right.

words.meaning: A sentence that asks. It ends with a question mark.
words.example: Can I ask a question?
practice: Write three questions for the form.
Answer the question in a sentence.
Where is it? That is a question.
What is the first question?
A question ends with a question mark.
words.tutor: Say a sentence that tells, like The class is on Monday. Ask the tutor to make it a question, then say both out loud.

words.meaning: The small point at the end of a sentence that tells.
words.example: Put a full stop at the end.
practice: I am Nadia. That sentence has a full stop.
Did you forget the full stop?
A question has no full stop.
Two sentences, two full stops.
Put a full stop after the last word.
words.tutor: Type three sentences for the tutor with no full stops and no question marks. Say which ones tell and which ones ask, then add the marks.

words.meaning: A small mark between the things in a list.
words.example: Bread, milk and eggs: the comma comes after bread.
practice: Put a comma after Hello Sam.
Tea, coffee and milk: one comma.
A comma is not a full stop.
Where is the comma in this list?
Put a comma before but.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor four things in your bag. Write them as one list, and ask it to check the commas and the and.

words.meaning: What you write on. The pages of a book are paper.
words.example: Can I have some paper, please?
practice: Write it on paper.
The form is on white paper.
I have a pen and some paper.
Put the paper in your bag.
This paper is too small.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for three things you can write on paper, like a list or a note. Say each one in a sentence with paper in it.

words.meaning: Books have pages: page 1, page 2, page 3.
words.example: Open your book at page 12.
practice: The story is on page 5.
Write on a new page.
This notebook has 100 pages.
Look at the first page.
What is on page 20?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to say five page numbers between 20 and 100. Write each one as a word, then check them with it.

words.meaning: Words about people and what they did. It can be made up.
words.example: I read a short story last night.
practice: The story is about a lost notebook.
Tell me a story.
Write a story in five sentences.
Did you like the story?
The story has a happy end.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor a made-up story in four sentences. Use then two times. Ask it to check your past words, like went, had and saw.

words.meaning: Something you want to say, write or do.
words.example: I have an idea: tea and a film this evening.
practice: Write your ideas in a list.
My first idea is a postcard.
One sentence, one idea.
Is that your idea?
Join two ideas with but.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor you want to write a note. Say three ideas for it as a list, then make each idea a sentence.

words.meaning: A time when you learn one thing, at school, at work or at home.
words.example: My English lesson is on Monday.
practice: The lesson is at six o'clock.
This lesson has four cards.
I had a lesson yesterday.
The lesson is one hour long.
What did you learn today?
words.tutor: Tell the tutor the day and time of a made-up lesson. Check you said on for the day and at for the time.

words.meaning: The people who learn together. It is also the time they learn.
words.example: There are twelve people in my English class.
practice: My class is on Tuesday evening.
Our class has a new room.
Is Ivan in your class?
The class starts at seven.
Our English class is at the library.
words.tutor: Describe a made-up English class to the tutor: the day, the time and how many people. Use there are for the people.

words.meaning: Work you do at home after a lesson.
words.example: I did my homework at the kitchen table.
practice: Did you finish your homework?
The homework is on page 20.
I have no homework today.
I do my homework in the evening.
Check your homework with the key.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor about some made-up homework: what it is and when you did it. Say homework with no a before it and no s at the end.

words.meaning: Questions that check what you know.
words.example: I have an English test on Friday.
practice: The test has twelve questions.
I practise for my test every day.
Check your answers after the test.
The test is on Friday morning.
Did you finish the test?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for a short test: five words from this unit to spell. Write them, then check each letter with it.

words.meaning: A small book with empty pages. You write in it.
words.example: I write new words in my notebook.
practice: My notebook is blue.
Open your notebook at a new page.
Where is my notebook?
Write the date in your notebook.
I left my notebook on the bus.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor three things you can write in a notebook. Then say one sentence and one question with notebook in them.

words.meaning: A book of words from A to Z. It says what each word is.
words.example: Look for the word in a dictionary.
practice: My dictionary is on the shelf.
Check the spelling in a dictionary.
Words in a dictionary go from A to Z.
Can I borrow your dictionary?
The word is on page 30 of my dictionary.
words.starter: I look in a dictionary for …
words.tutor: Say four words from this unit. Put them in dictionary order yourself, from A to Z, then ask the tutor to check the order.

words.meaning: A thing that is not right.
words.example: I found a mistake: two full stops.
practice: Find the mistake in this sentence.
Sorry, my mistake!
Everyone makes mistakes.
Check your note for mistakes.
A mistake is OK. Fix it.
words.tutor: Ask the tutor for a sentence with one mistake in it. Find the mistake and fix it. Then ask for one more.

words.meaning: To do a thing again and again, to get better at it.
words.example: I practise my English every day.
practice: Practise the new words slowly.
She practises at night.
Did you practise yesterday?
We practise questions with a friend.
Practise the note, then write it.
words.tutor: Tell the tutor what you practise and when: English, a song or football. Ask it to check that practise has an s.

words.meaning: To get to know a new thing.
words.example: I learn ten new words every week.
practice: I learned to swim last year.
What did you learn today?
We learn English on Saturday.
Learn one pattern, then practise it.
Where did you learn English?
words.tutor: Tell the tutor three things you learned this week. Start each one with I learned, and say the -ed end short.

words.meaning: To still know it later: a name, a word, a time.
words.example: I remember her name: it is Zoe.
practice: Remember your full stops!
Do you remember my phone number?
I can't remember the word.
Remember to bring your notebook.
Did you remember the homework?
words.tutor: Ask the tutor to say five new words. Wait one minute. Say the words you remember, and check which ones you did not.

words.meaning: Not to remember: a name, a key, a full stop. The past is forgot.
words.example: Don't forget your pen.
practice: I forgot my notebook at home.
Did you forget the question mark?
Don't forget to call Sam.
I forget new words quickly.
Sorry, I forgot your name.
words.tutor: Forget is forgot in the past. Tell the tutor three made-up things you forgot, like I forgot my keys.

grammar.title: But, or, then: join two ideas
grammar.explanation:
And joins two things. Now three more joining words.
But: the second idea is different.
Or: you choose one.
Then: this one comes after.
grammar.rule:
and — I like tea and coffee.
but — I like tea, but I don't like coffee.
but — I can read the word, but I can't say it.
or — Tea or coffee?
or — We can walk, or we can take the bus.
then — I did my homework. Then I went to bed.
then — Read the note, then call Sam.

A comma before but.
Then can start a sentence: Then I went to bed.
grammar.workedExample:
Join: I can read the word. I can't say it.
1. Idea one: I can read the word.
2. Idea two: I can't say it.
3. Can, then can't: the ideas are different.
4. Different ideas: but.
5. Write: I can read the word, but I can't say it.
6. Check: a comma before but. Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to use and for everything.
No: I like tea and I don't like coffee.
Yes: I like tea, but I don't like coffee.
A yes and a no: use but.
grammar.tip: And adds. But changes. Or chooses. Then comes after.
grammar.practice:
Write one: and, but, or, then.
1. I have a pen, ___ I don't have paper.
2. Is the test on Monday ___ on Tuesday?
3. I read the story. ___ I answered three questions.
4. I like the lesson, ___ the homework is long.
5. Do you want tea ___ coffee?
6. I got bread ___ milk at the shop.
7. Plan your note first. ___ write it.
grammar.answers:
1. but  2. or  3. Then  4. but  5. or  6. and  7. Then
Wrong on 1 or 4? The two ideas are different, so but.
Wrong on 6? Two things you got, no change: and.
Then starts a sentence in 3 and 7, so it has a capital.

grammar.title: A capital at the start: names, places, days
grammar.explanation:
Some words always start with a capital.
Names, places, days, months and languages.
The first word of a sentence.
And the word I.
grammar.rule:
The first word: My bag is red.
A name: Nadia, Tomas, Zoe.
A place name: Park Street, the Star Café.
A day: Monday, Friday.
A month: May, October.
A language: English.
I: Can I help? Yes, I can.

No name: small.
a street, a café, a bank, a city
With a name: capitals.
Park Street, the Star Café
grammar.workedExample:
Fix it: on monday, sam went to park street.
1. On is the first word: On.
2. Monday is a day: Monday.
3. Sam is a name: Sam.
4. Park Street is a place name: Park Street.
5. Write: On Monday, Sam went to Park Street.
6. Check: four capitals. Yes.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to put a capital on street or city.
No: I live on a Street in the City.
Yes: I live on a street in the city.
A capital is for the name: Park Street.
grammar.tip: Names, places, days, months, English, I and the first word: capitals.
grammar.practice:
Write each sentence again, with capitals.
1. my class is on tuesday.
2. zoe lives on hill street.
3. i have a test in june.
4. we had tea at the star café.
5. can omar come on friday?
6. the library is next to a bank.
grammar.answers:
1. My class is on Tuesday.
2. Zoe lives on Hill Street.
3. I have a test in June.
4. We had tea at the Star Café.
5. Can Omar come on Friday?
6. The library is next to a bank.
Count your capitals: 2, 3, 2, 3, 3, 1.
Wrong on 6? A bank with no name stays small.

grammar.title: Full stop or question mark?
grammar.explanation:
A sentence that tells ends with a full stop.
A sentence that asks ends with a question mark.
In a list, a comma goes between the things.
grammar.rule:
Tells: The test is on Friday.
Asks: Is the test on Friday?

Tells: She lives here.
Asks: Where does she live?

Tells: You can come.
Asks: Can you come?

These start questions:
what, where, when, who, why, how
do, does, did, can, is, are

A list: bread, milk and eggs.
grammar.workedExample:
Full stop or question mark?
Did you remember the paper
1. Look at the first word: Did.
2. Did starts a question.
3. So the sentence asks.
4. Write: Did you remember the paper?
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to put a full stop on a question.
No: Where is my notebook.
Yes: Where is my notebook?
Where is the first word, so it asks.
No: I forgot my pen?
Yes: I forgot my pen.
grammar.tip: It asks: a question mark. It tells: a full stop.
grammar.practice:
Write a full stop or a question mark.
1. Where is the post office
2. The lesson starts at six
3. Do you have a dictionary
4. I forgot my homework
5. Can I borrow your pen
6. Nadia found one mistake
7. Why are you late
grammar.answers:
1. question mark  2. full stop  3. question mark  4. full stop  5. question mark  6. full stop  7. question mark
Wrong on 4? It tells, so a full stop. I is not a question word.
Look at the first word: where, do, can and why start questions.

grammar.title: Plan, write, check: a short note
grammar.explanation:
Write in three steps.
Plan: write your ideas as a list.
Write: one idea in each sentence.
Check: read it again and fix the mistakes.
grammar.rule:
1. Plan
Who is it for? Sam.
Why? I am late.
Ideas: late, at the bank, home at seven.

2. Write
Hello Sam,
I am at the bank, and I will be late.
I will be home at seven.
Nadia

3. Check
Capitals: names, places, days, the first word.
The end: a full stop or a question mark.
Spelling: check new words in a dictionary.
grammar.workedExample:
Check this line.
i am at the market, but i will be home soon
1. Capitals: i is I. It is the first word too: I.
2. The second i: I.
3. The end: it tells, so a full stop.
4. Spelling: market. Check it. Yes.
5. Write: I am at the market, but I will be home soon.
grammar.mistake:
It is easy to stop after step 2.
Read your note again, line by line.
Look for one thing at a time.
First capitals, then the ends, then spelling.
grammar.tip: Plan it. Write it. Check it.
grammar.practice:
Check the postcard. Find 7 mistakes.
1. hello Tomas,
2. i am in a big city
3. Yesterday I visited a market, then I had tea.
4. Today I will go to the cinema?
5. do you like my postcard
6. from Yara
grammar.answers:
1. Hello Tomas,
2. I am in a big city.
3. No mistake.
4. Today I will go to the cinema.
5. Do you like my postcard?
6. From Yara
The 7: Hello, I, Do and From need capitals.
Lines 2 and 4 need a full stop. Line 5 needs a question mark.
Missed number 4? It tells, so a full stop, not a question mark.

readings.title: Nadia's Notebook
readings.setting: An English class, a café and a test, over two days.
readings.passage:
Nadia has an English class on Tuesday evening.
She writes new words in a small green notebook.
Then she writes a sentence for each word.
On Monday, she left the notebook at a café.
All her new words are in it. The test is on Tuesday!
She called the café, then she went there.
The man at the café gave her the notebook.
“Is this yours?” he asked.
“Yes! Thanks!” said Nadia.
That evening, she read her words again.
On Tuesday, she didn't forget one word.

readings.title: How to Write a Short Note
readings.setting: Three steps for a note to a friend or someone at home.
readings.passage:
A note is short. Three or four sentences are OK.
First, plan. Who is it for? Why do you write it?
Write your ideas as a list.
Then write. Start with hello and the name: Hello Sam,
Write one idea in each sentence.
Join two ideas with and, but, or or then.
At the end, write your name.
Last, check. Read it again.
Capitals? Full stops? Question marks?
Is a word new? Check it in a dictionary.

readings.title: English Class at the Library
readings.setting: A notice on the wall of a library.
readings.passage:
ENGLISH CLASS AT THE LIBRARY
Every Wednesday, 6 o'clock to 7 o'clock, Room 3.
The class is for everyone. You don't pay.

Please bring:
a notebook
a pen or a pencil

No dictionary? The library has ten. You can borrow one.

Homework: one page every week.
A short test: the last Wednesday of the month.

New? Please write your name on the form at the front desk.

comprehension.why: Line 1: Nadia has an English class on Tuesday evening.

comprehension.q: Where did Nadia leave her notebook?
comprehension.why: Line 4: On Monday, she left the notebook at a café.

comprehension.q: Why did Nadia want the notebook back on Monday?
comprehension.a: Her new words are in it. The test is on Tuesday.
comprehension.why: Line 5: All her new words are in it. The test is on Tuesday!

comprehension.q: What is the story about? A café, a lost notebook or a new pen?
comprehension.why: Nadia leaves her notebook, then gets it back. The café is only the place.

comprehension.q: What are the three steps for a note?
comprehension.why: The guide says: First, plan. Then write. Last, check.

comprehension.q: The guide says: Last, check. What does last mean here?
comprehension.a: The third step, after plan and write.
comprehension.why: First, plan. Then write. Last, check. Last is the step at the end.

comprehension.q: You are not sure how to spell a word. What do you do?
comprehension.why: Last line: Is a word new? Check it in a dictionary.

comprehension.q: What day is the class, and at what time?
comprehension.a: On Wednesday, from 6 o'clock to 7 o'clock.
comprehension.why: Line 2: Every Wednesday, 6 o'clock to 7 o'clock.

comprehension.q: You want to go to the class. What do you bring?
comprehension.a: A notebook, and a pen or a pencil.
comprehension.why: Please bring: a notebook, a pen or a pencil.

comprehension.q: You are new, and you have no dictionary. What do you do?
comprehension.a: Write your name on the form at the front desk. Borrow a dictionary at the library.
comprehension.why: New? Please write your name on the form. No dictionary? The library has ten. You can borrow one.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — But, or, then
speaking.instructions:
Listen. Say each line.
I like tea, but I don't like coffee.
Tea or coffee?
We can walk, or we can take the bus.
I read the note. Then I called Sam.
I can read the word, but I can't say it.
First I plan, then I write.
Tap the mic. Say the 6 lines.
Tap again. Listen.
Check: a small stop before but? But, or or then in every line?
speaking.tutor: Say one idea to the tutor, like I like music. Ask for a second idea. Join them with but, or or then.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — My evening, step by step
speaking.instructions:
Say 5 lines about one evening.
Use then in 3 lines and but in 1 line.
Listen to the model.
I got home at six.
Then I cooked rice.
Then I did my homework.
I like films, but I didn't watch one.
Then I went to bed.
It can be after school or after work.
You can make it up.
Tap the mic. Say your 5 lines. Tap again. Listen.
Check: 5 lines? Then 3 times? But 1 time?
speaking.tutor: Say your five lines to the tutor. Ask it to mix up the order. Then put them back in order.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Tea or coffee?
speaking.instructions:
Read A. Say B.
1. A: Tea or coffee? B: Tea, please.
2. A: Is the class on Monday or Tuesday? B: It is on Tuesday.
3. A: A pen or a pencil? B: A pencil, please.
4. A: Do you want a list or a note? B: A list, thanks.
5. A: Now or later? B: Later, please.
Tap the mic. Say the 5 B lines. Tap again. Listen.
Check: did you choose one thing in each B line?
A friend can say A. No one with you? Say A and B.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor five questions with or, like Tea or coffee? Then answer five of its questions. Choose one thing each time.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Listen and do
speaking.instructions:
Take a paper and a pen.
Listen. Do each step.
1. Write a name. A made-up name is OK.
2. Then write a day, like Monday.
3. Write one sentence about your bag.
4. Then write one question for a friend.
Now check your paper.
A capital on the name and the day?
A full stop after the sentence?
A question mark after the question?
Tap the mic. Read your paper out loud. Tap again. Listen.
This is one model paper.
Zoe
Friday
My bag is black.
Do you like my bag?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for four new writing steps, one at a time. Do each one on paper. Then read your paper to it.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Read the note out loud
speaking.instructions:
Read this note out loud.
Hello Sam,
I am at the library, but I will be home at seven.
Can you get bread and milk?
Then we can cook.
Thanks!
Nadia
Stop a little at each full stop.
Say the question like a question.
Tap the mic. Read it. Tap again. Listen.
Check: a small stop at each full stop? A small stop before but? Did the question sound like a question?
speaking.tutor: Read the note to the tutor. Ask: Did I stop at each full stop? Then read it again.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — At the library desk
speaking.instructions:
You want to go to the English class at the library.
Listen. Say your lines.
Desk: Hello! Can I help you?
You: Yes, please. When is the English class?
Desk: On Wednesday, at six o'clock.
You: Can I borrow a dictionary there?
Desk: Yes, you can. There are ten.
You: Thanks. Can I have a form, please?
Desk: Here you are. Did you bring a pen?
You: No, I didn't. Can I borrow one?
Desk: Sure. Here you are.
You: Thanks! Goodbye.
You can use a made-up name on the form.
Tap the mic. Say your lines. Tap again. Listen.
Check: 5 lines? One question with when? Can in 3 lines? Didn't in your answer?
A friend can read the desk lines. No one with you? Read them and answer.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be the person at the library desk. Ask it when the class is, and ask to borrow two things.

writing.title: Writing 1 — Two ideas in one sentence
writing.prompt:
Write 4 sentences about you.
Join two ideas in each one.
Use and, but, or and then: one of each.
You can make it up.
writing.model:
I like tea and coffee.
I can read English, but I can't spell every word.
On Saturday, I study or I go to the park.
I do my homework, then I go to bed.
writing.criteria:
4 sentences.
And, but, or and then: one of each.
A comma before but.
A capital letter at the start of each.
A full stop at the end of each.
writing.support:
Copy the model.
In each sentence, change one idea.
Keep the joining word.
writing.extension: Write one question with or, like Tea or coffee?

writing.title: Writing 2 — A note for someone at home
writing.prompt:
Write a note for a friend or someone in your family.
Plan first: who, why, and a list of ideas.
Then write 4 sentences.
Then check it.
writing.model:
Plan: Ben, I am late, the market, eggs?

Hello Ben,
I am at the market, and I will be late.
There are no eggs at home.
Can you get some?
Then we can cook.
Yara
writing.criteria:
A plan with 3 ideas or more.
Hello and a name at the start. Your name at the end.
4 sentences.
One question, with a question mark.
You checked 3 things: capitals, the ends, spelling.
writing.support:
Copy the model.
Change the name, the place and the food.
Then check one thing at a time: capitals first.
writing.extension: Write a thanks note to a person who helped you. Use but one time.

writing.title: Writing 3 — A postcard from a visit
writing.prompt:
You visit a new place. Write a postcard to a friend.
Use names: a person, a place and a day.
Write it by hand.
You can make up the place.
writing.model:
Hello Zoe,
I am in a big city.
On Monday, I visited Green Park.
There is a big market on King Street.
Yesterday I ate fish at the Blue Café.
See you on Friday!
Tomas
writing.criteria:
6 lines and your name.
A capital on every name, place and day: 5 or more.
Each sentence ends with a full stop or a question mark.
One line with there is or there are.
By hand: small letters all one size, and a space between words.
writing.support:
First write the names: a friend, two places, a day.
Put a capital on each one.
Then copy the model and put your names in.
writing.extension: Add an address: a number, a street name, a city name.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Questions for the English class
writing.prompt:
Read the notice in Reading 3.
Write 4 questions about the class.
Then answer each one from the notice.
writing.model:
When is the class? It is on Wednesday.
What time does it start? It starts at six o'clock.
Can I borrow a dictionary? Yes, you can.
Is there a test? Yes, on the last Wednesday of the month.
writing.criteria:
4 questions, each with a question mark.
4 answers, each with a full stop.
4 different first words.
Every answer is in the notice.
writing.support:
Start your questions with these: When, What time, Can I, Is there.
Find each answer in the notice and copy it.
writing.extension: Write one question the notice does not answer. Example: Is the room big?

activities.title: Practice 1 — And, but, or, then
activities.instructions:
Write one: and, but, or, then.
1. I have a notebook ___ a dictionary.
2. I remember the word, ___ I can't spell it.
3. Do you practise in the morning ___ at night?
4. Plan your note. ___ write it.
5. The lesson is short, ___ the homework is long.
6. Is it a note ___ a list?
7. I did the homework. ___ I checked it.
8. I got milk, eggs ___ bread.
activities.answers:
1. and  2. but  3. or  4. Then  5. but  6. or  7. Then  8. and
Wrong on 2 or 5? Different ideas: but.
Wrong on 3 or 6? You choose one: or.
7 or 8 right: good.
6 or less: read Pattern 1 and do it again.
activities.solo: Say each sentence out loud with each word. Write the one that fits. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Join the two sentences
activities.instructions:
Make one sentence. Use the word in brackets.
1. I like the lesson. I don't like the test. (but)
2. Do you want a list? Do you want a note? (or)
3. I read the story. I answered a question. (then)
4. I have a pen. I have paper. (and)
5. I can speak English. I can't spell long words. (but)
6. We can meet on Monday. We can meet on Friday. (or)
activities.answers:
1. I like the lesson, but I don't like the test.
2. Do you want a list or a note?
3. I read the story, then I answered a question.
4. I have a pen and paper.
5. I can speak English, but I can't spell long words.
6. We can meet on Monday or on Friday.
In 2, 4 and 6, you don't need the same words two times.
Also right: We can meet on Monday, or we can meet on Friday.
5 or 6 right: good.
4 or less: read Pattern 1 again.
activities.solo: Write each new sentence. Read it out loud. Check with the key and count.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Put in the capitals
activities.instructions:
Some capitals are missing. Write each sentence again.
1. my sister lives in a small village.
2. we have a test on thursday.
3. can i borrow your notebook?
4. ivan works at the post office on king street.
5. my english class is in march.
6. the cinema is next to the star café.
7. yara and omar went to the library on friday.
8. is the lesson in may or june?
activities.answers:
1. My sister lives in a small village.
2. We have a test on Thursday.
3. Can I borrow your notebook?
4. Ivan works at the post office on King Street.
5. My English class is in March.
6. The cinema is next to the Star Café.
7. Yara and Omar went to the library on Friday.
8. Is the lesson in May or June?
Count your capitals: 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3.
Number 1: a village with no name stays small.
Number 5: English is a language, so it has a capital.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read Pattern 2 again.
activities.solo: Write each sentence. Then count your capitals and check the count with the key.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Full stops, question marks and commas
activities.instructions:
Write the mark: a full stop, a question mark or a comma.
1. Where is the dictionary ___
2. I forgot my homework ___
3. Please bring paper ___ a pen and a notebook.
4. Did you remember the test ___
5. Hello Sam ___ (the first line of a note)
6. The lesson is on page 20 ___
7. Tea ___ coffee or milk?
8. Can you check my postcard ___
activities.answers:
1. question mark  2. full stop  3. comma  4. question mark  5. comma  6. full stop  7. comma  8. question mark
Number 3: in a list, a comma goes between things. No comma before and.
Number 7 asks, so it ends with a question mark. The comma goes after tea.
7 or 8 right: good. 6 or less: read Pattern 3 again.
activities.solo: Read each line out loud. Does it ask or tell? Write the mark. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Space the words
activities.instructions:
The spaces are gone. Write each line again.
Add spaces and capitals.
End with a full stop or a question mark.
1. iliketea
2. whereismynotebook
3. samlivesonparkstreet
4. myclassisonmonday
5. didyoufinishthetest
6. ileftanoteforzoe
activities.answers:
1. I like tea.
2. Where is my notebook?
3. Sam lives on Park Street.
4. My class is on Monday.
5. Did you finish the test?
6. I left a note for Zoe.
Now look at your own writing. Is there a space between every two words?
5 or 6 right: good. 4 or less: say each line slowly. Write one word at a time.
activities.solo: Say each line out loud, slowly. Write a space after each word you hear. Check with the key.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Units 7 to 12 check
activities.instructions:
Choose the right word. These patterns come from Units 7 to 12.
1. ___ you have a dictionary? (Do / Does)
2. There ___ two notebooks on the desk. (is / are)
3. This is ___ notebook. (Nadia / Nadia's)
4. Yesterday I ___ my homework. (finish / finished)
5. ___ you go to the lesson last week? (Do / Did)
6. Can I borrow your pen? ___ (Here you are. / Yes, I do.)
7. I'll ___ you a postcard. (send / sent)
8. I cut the paper ___ scissors. (with / for)
9. The lesson is ___ six o'clock. (at / in)
activities.answers:
1. Do (Unit 7)  2. are (Unit 8)  3. Nadia's (Unit 8)  4. finished (Unit 10)  5. Did (Unit 10)  6. Here you are. (Unit 11)  7. send (Unit 11)  8. with (Unit 12)  9. at (Unit 11)
Wrong on 5? Last week is the past, so did.
Wrong on 7? After I'll, the word does not change: send.
8 or 9 right: good.
7 or less: find the unit of each wrong answer. Read its pattern card again.
activities.solo: Write your answers. Check with the key. Write down the unit of each wrong answer.

quizzes.q: I like tea, ___ I don't like coffee.
quizzes.why: Like and don't like are different ideas, so but. And joins two things with no change. Or is for a choice. Then is for what comes after.

quizzes.q: Is your class on Monday ___ on Friday?
quizzes.why: The question asks you to choose one day, so or. Then is for what comes after. But is for different ideas. At is for a clock time.

quizzes.q: I did my homework. ___ I went to bed.
quizzes.why: Bed comes after the homework, so then. Or is for a choice. Where starts a question. Of does not join two ideas.
I is always a capital, and Park Street is a place name. Live and on are not names, so they stay small.

quizzes.q: Which word always starts with a capital?
quizzes.why: Monday is a day, and days always have a capital. Street and city have a capital only in a name, like Park Street. A bag never does.

quizzes.q: Which one needs a question mark?
options: The pen is on the desk
quizzes.why: Where starts a question, so it asks. I forgot my pen tells. Write with a pen tells you what to do. The pen is on the desk tells.

quizzes.q: Bread ___ milk and eggs. What goes after bread?
quizzes.why: In a list, a comma goes between the things. A full stop ends a sentence. A question mark ends a question. A capital is a letter, not a mark.

quizzes.q: Check this note: hello Sam, I am at the bank. What is the mistake?
quizzes.why: Hello is the first word, so it needs a capital. Sam is a name, so its capital is right. The sentence tells, so a full stop is right. A bank with no name stays small.
She is one person, so does: Does she live here? Do is for I, you, we and they. Is and are go with -ing: Is she living here?

quizzes.q: There ___ three dictionaries on the shelf. (Unit 8)
quizzes.why: Three dictionaries are more than one, so there are. There is is for one thing. Am is only for I. Be does not go here.

quizzes.q: Yesterday I ___ my notebook on the bus. (Unit 10)
quizzes.why: Yesterday is the past. Leave changes to left, with no -ed. Leave and leaves are for now. Leaving needs am or is.
Sam gets the postcard, so for: a present for you. With is for the thing you use, or the person with you. Of and at do not fit here.

teacherNotes.note: Every card has a worked example before its practice, every exercise has a key with a score line, and every writing task ends in a visible checklist the learner counts against. The check step is deliberately split into one thing at a time (capitals, then end marks, then spelling), because a beginner asked to check everything at once checks nothing. If you are helping, ask the learner which of the three they checked, rather than marking the page for them.

This is the last unit of Stage 2. Quiz items 9 to 12 and Practice 6 revisit Units 7 to 12 (do and does, there are, possessive 's, the past, can I and here you are, will, with and for, at for clock times), and the assignment draws on the whole stage. Practice 6 names the unit beside each answer. Two or more wrong from one unit is the signal to revisit that unit's card before Unit 14.

Most of this unit's skills are writing mechanics: capitals, full stops, question marks, joining, planning, and letters of one size with a space between words. The evidence is on paper. Writing 3 asks for handwriting; if you are helping, look at the size of the small letters and the spaces, which the learner can see and count for themselves.

Because is Level 1 Unit 19; first, next and finally as a sequence are Unit 15. Speech marks and the apostrophe rules are not taught; the exclamation mark appears in models but is not taught. Irregular pasts not yet taught (wrote, made, bought) are avoided; forgot is given with forget as a word form. Practise with an s is the UK verb; the app's Practice section is the noun.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service, and no task is scored by it alone. Notes, postcards and forms here use made-up names, places and details throughout, and the learner is told so. Never ask the learner to give the tutor a real address or phone number.

selfAssessment.statement: I can join two ideas with but, or and then.
I can say what I did, step by step, with then.
I can put capitals on names, places and days.
I can end a sentence with a full stop or a question mark.
I can plan, write and check a short note.
I can read a short story and say what it is about.
I can listen to four steps and do them.
I can ask and answer at a desk: When is it? Can I borrow one?

assignment.title: My week, said and written
assignment.instructions:
Two parts. They use Units 7 to 13.
1. Tap the mic. Say 5 lines about last week. Say where you went and what you did. Use but one time and then one time. Ask one question with Did you, and answer it.
2. Write a postcard to a friend, 6 lines. Plan it, write it, then check it. Use a name, a place and a day. Write one line with there is or there are, and one question.
You can make up the place, the people and the week.
assignment.submissionType: Audio recording and a written postcard
